tagline: The second half of the Chronicler's history: Solomon's temple, the kings of Judah, the fall of Jerusalem, and a closing word of return.
overview:
Second Chronicles picks up where First Chronicles ends, with Solomon on David's throne. Its first nine chapters are almost entirely about one project: the building and dedication of the temple in Jerusalem, the house where the LORD chose to put his name. The remaining twenty-seven chapters follow the kings of Judah, the southern kingdom ruled by David's descendants, from the split of the nation under Rehoboam to the burning of the temple by the Babylonians in 587 or 586 BC. The northern kingdom of Israel appears mostly at the edges, when it touches Judah's story.

The book covers much of the same ground as 1 and 2 Kings, often in the same words, but it is not a copy. It was written later, for a small community of Jews back in the land after the exile, and it tells the old story to answer their questions. Are we still God's people? Does the promise to David still stand? What does faithfulness look like with a rebuilt temple and no king? So the Chronicler lingers over worship, the Levites and singers, Passover celebrations, and the reforms of kings like Hezekiah and Josiah. He shows kings who seek the LORD being helped and kings who abandon him being disciplined, often within the same reign, and he tells of repentance that God answers, most strikingly in the case of Manasseh.

The book ends not with the ashes of Jerusalem but with a decree. Cyrus king of Persia, stirred by the LORD, invites the people to go up and build the house of God again. In the traditional Jewish order of the Hebrew Bible, Chronicles is the last book, so the whole Hebrew Scripture closes on the words “and may he go up” (36:23), a door left open.
author:
The book doesn't name its author. Chronicles was originally one work (the division into two books comes from the Greek translation, the Septuagint, and was later taken into Hebrew Bibles). Jewish tradition in the Babylonian Talmud credited Ezra with writing Chronicles, and for a long time scholars treated Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah as one continuous history by a single author, partly because the end of Chronicles (36:22-23) and the start of Ezra (1:1-3) share the same decree of Cyrus. Since the late twentieth century many scholars, notably Sara Japhet and H. G. M. Williamson, have argued on grounds of vocabulary and outlook that Chronicles and Ezra-Nehemiah come from different hands. Most now speak simply of "the Chronicler". His deep interest in the Levites, the temple singers, and the gatekeepers has led many to think he was a Levite himself, though that is an inference.

The Chronicler was a careful user of sources. He drew heavily on the books of Samuel and Kings, in a form sometimes closer to Hebrew manuscripts found among the Dead Sea Scrolls than to the traditional Hebrew text, and he cites other works by name, such as the records of Nathan the prophet and the visions of Iddo the seer (9:29), which have not survived.
date: Chronicles was written after the exile, since it ends with Cyrus's decree of 539/538 BC and its genealogy of David's line (1 Chronicles 3) runs several generations past Zerubbabel, the governor who led the return. It also mentions darics (1 Chronicles 29:7), a Persian gold coin first minted around the end of the sixth century BC. Most scholars date the book somewhere in the Persian period, commonly around 400 to 350 BC. Some place it a little later, in the early Greek period after Alexander the Great, and a minority have argued for a first edition as early as about 520 to 500 BC, connected with the rebuilding of the temple. Its stories, of course, are set much earlier, from Solomon's accession around 970 BC to the fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC.
setting:
The events of 2 Chronicles run through four centuries of the southern kingdom. Solomon reigned over a united Israel in the tenth century BC with wide trade links to Tyre, Egypt, Arabia, and beyond. After his death the ten northern tribes broke away under Jeroboam, and Judah, with Benjamin and much of the priesthood, remained under David's line in Jerusalem. Judah lived in the shadow of greater powers: Egypt (the Pharaoh Shishak invaded under Rehoboam), then Assyria (which destroyed the northern kingdom and fell on Judah under Hezekiah in 701 BC), and finally Babylon, whose king Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem and burned the temple.

The first readers lived in a very different world. Judah was now Yehud, a small province of the Persian Empire. The temple had been rebuilt, completed in 516/515 BC, but it was modest, there was no Davidic king on the throne, and the community was poor, small, and often discouraged. Priests and Levites carried much of the nation's leadership. For these readers the story of the old temple and the old kings was not antiquarian interest. It told them who they were and how to live before God in their own day.
purpose: The Chronicler wrote to encourage and instruct the restored community in Jerusalem. He wanted them to see that they were the continuation of "all Israel", heirs of the promises to David and of the worship David and Solomon established, and that the temple they served in was the center of their life with God. He also wanted them to learn from their history. Again and again he shows that seeking the LORD brings help and that forsaking him brings trouble, and above all that God answers those who humble themselves and return. The prayer of Solomon and God's reply in chapters 6 and 7 work almost as the book's program, and the stories that follow show it being tested in reign after reign. His goal was hope grounded in faithfulness: the God who judged Jerusalem had also brought his people back, and the door to him remained open.
story: Second Chronicles continues First Chronicles, which traced the family of Adam to the tribes of Israel and then told David's reign with a focus on the ark and his preparations for the temple. Here Solomon builds what David planned, and the story then moves through the kings of Judah until the exile. It covers the same period as 1 Kings 1 through 2 Kings 25 but from another angle. What follows it historically is told in Ezra and Nehemiah: the return from Babylon, the rebuilding of the temple and walls, and the reforming of the community. The prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, Micah, and others spoke into the reigns narrated here, and reading them alongside this book fills out the picture.
christ: Chronicles is a book about a king and a temple, and the New Testament presents Jesus as the fulfillment of both. The promise to David that his son would build God's house and that his throne would last forever (1 Chronicles 17) hangs over every king in this book, and each falls short; the line ends in exile. The Gospels open by presenting Jesus as the son of David, and Matthew's genealogy, like Chronicles, tells Israel's history as a sequence of generations through David and the exile. Jesus also speaks of his own body as the temple (John 2:19-21), the place where God dwells among his people, and the New Testament goes on to call the church God's temple built on him. Many interpreters also note that when Jesus spoke of the blood of the prophets from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah (Luke 11:51), he may have been reaching from the first murder in Genesis to the murder of the prophet Zechariah in the temple court in 2 Chronicles 24, first and last in the Hebrew order of books, though the identification is discussed. The book's closing summons to go up and build is fulfilled in part by the return from exile, and the New Testament sees its deeper answer in the one who gathers God's people into a house not made with hands.
reading:
Read Chronicles as a sermon on history, not as a second draft of Kings. Where you have both accounts, comparing them is rewarding: notice what the Chronicler leaves out (David's adultery, most of Solomon's fall into idolatry, nearly all of the northern kings), what he adds (speeches, prophets, reforms, Passovers, the repentance of Manasseh), and how he frames it. These choices are his message. He is not hiding the failures, which his readers knew well from Samuel and Kings; he is drawing out what they needed to hear.

Watch for his key words: "seek" the LORD, "forsake" or "abandon" him, "humble" oneself, "unfaithful", and "all Israel". Watch too for the pattern in which a king's faithfulness brings rest, building, and victory, while unfaithfulness brings defeat or illness. A common misreading takes this as a mechanical rule that every blessing proves obedience and every trouble proves sin. The Chronicler's point is more pastoral: God responds to his people, repentance is never wasted, and each generation stands before God on its own account. The large numbers in the book (armies, offerings, sums of gold) are a known difficulty; some reflect a word for "thousand" that may also mean a military unit, some may be scribal, and some may be deliberate grandeur, and interpreters weigh these options differently.

structure.title: Solomon and the temple
structure.summary: Solomon receives wisdom, builds and furnishes the temple, brings in the ark, prays at its dedication, and is answered by fire and glory. His wealth and fame draw the queen of Sheba and the nations.

structure.title: The kingdom divides
structure.summary: Rehoboam's harsh answer splits the nation. Judah is strengthened, then abandons the law, and is humbled by Shishak of Egypt.

structure.title: Abijah, Asa, and Jehoshaphat
structure.summary: Kings who seek the LORD find help in battle and lead reforms, though Asa ends badly and Jehoshaphat makes unwise alliances with the north.

structure.title: From Jehoram to Ahaz
structure.summary: Alliance with Ahab's house brings Athaliah's usurpation, Joash's rescue and later apostasy, and a line of kings who begin well and end poorly, down to Ahaz, who shuts the temple doors.

structure.title: Hezekiah's reform
structure.summary: Hezekiah reopens and cleanses the temple, invites all Israel to Passover, and is delivered from Sennacherib of Assyria.

structure.title: Manasseh to the exile, and a decree
structure.summary: Manasseh sins greatly and repents in captivity, Josiah renews the covenant, the last kings fall, Jerusalem is burned, and Cyrus invites the exiles to go up.

themes.title: The temple and worship
themes.body: The temple is the book's center of gravity. Solomon's building occupies nine chapters, and the kings who follow are judged largely by how they treat it: Asa, Joash, Hezekiah, and Josiah restore and cleanse it, while Ahaz shuts its doors and Manasseh fills it with idols. The Chronicler dwells on the Levites, the singers, the gatekeepers, and the festivals, because for his readers the rebuilt temple and its worship were where their identity as God's people was lived out.

themes.title: Seeking the LORD
themes.body: The verb "seek" runs through the book as its measure of a king. To seek the LORD is to turn toward him in worship, obedience, and trust, especially in a crisis. Kings who seek him are helped; kings who forsake him are forsaken. The pattern is stated in God's reply to Solomon, “if My people who are called by My name humble themselves and pray and seek My face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land” (7:14), and the rest of the book tests it reign by reign.

themes.title: Repentance and mercy
themes.body: The Chronicler is the Old Testament's great narrator of turning back. Rehoboam and his officials humble themselves and are spared destruction; Hezekiah invites the north to return; and Manasseh, the worst king of all in Kings, is shown in Chronicles taken captive, praying, and restored, so that “Manasseh knew that the LORD is God” (33:13). For a community that had lived through judgment, this was the heart of the message: God receives those who return.

themes.title: All Israel and the house of David
themes.body: Though the book follows Judah, the Chronicler keeps speaking of "all Israel". He does not write the northern tribes off; Abijah appeals to them, Hezekiah invites them, and Josiah's reform reaches their territory. At the same time he holds to God's promise to David's line, the lamp that God will not put out. The restored community had no king, and the book keeps that promise alive.

themes.title: The prophets as God's voice
themes.body: Prophets and seers appear at nearly every turn: Shemaiah, who is also known from Kings, and many known only from Chronicles, such as Azariah son of Oded, Hanani, Jahaziel, Zechariah son of Jehoiada, Oded. They warn, encourage, and interpret events. Their presence shows that judgment never came without warning, a point the closing chapter makes explicitly: the LORD sent messengers again and again “because He had compassion on them and on His dwelling place” (36:15).

keyChapters.why: Solomon asks for wisdom at Gibeon, and the Chronicler sets the tone for his reign: a king whose greatness is God's gift.
Solomon's dedication prayer asks God to hear from heaven whenever his people pray toward this house, a prayer the rest of the book tests.
Fire and glory fill the temple, and God answers Solomon with the promise of 7:14 and a warning of exile.
Rehoboam's harsh answer divides the kingdom, a turning point the Chronicler traces to God's word through Ahijah.
Jehoshaphat's prayer in the face of invasion and the victory won by singing show the book's theology of trust in its clearest form.
Hezekiah's Passover invites all Israel, north and south, back to the house of God, and God heals a people who were not ritually ready.
Manasseh's captivity, prayer, and restoration show that no one is beyond the reach of repentance.
Jerusalem falls after long mercy, the land keeps its Sabbaths, and Cyrus's decree leaves the door open for return.
